title: HE WORE PURPLE. LAZARUS WORE SORES. THEN DEATH REVEALED WHO WAS TRULY RICH.
paragraphs: HE WORE PURPLE. LAZARUS WORE SORES. THEN DEATH REVEALED WHO WAS TRULY RICH.
The terrifying truth behind Jesus’ story of the rich man and Lazarus—and why the greatest tragedy wasn't the wealth he possessed, but the mercy he refused to show while eternity was approaching.
There was a man who had everything money could buy.
Beautiful clothes. Expensive meals. A comfortable home. People who probably knew his name, admired his success, and wished they could live his life.
And just outside his gate, another man was dying.
Not in some distant country.
Not in a neighborhood he had never visited.
Right outside his gate.
His name was Lazarus.
He was hungry. His body was covered in sores. He longed for scraps from the rich man's table. Even the dogs came and licked his wounds.
And every day, life continued.
The rich man ate.
Lazarus suffered.
The rich man dressed in luxury.
Lazarus lay in misery.
The rich man had more than enough.
Lazarus was longing for what fell from the table.
Then something happened that neither man's wealth nor poverty could prevent.
They both died.
And Jesus revealed something so disturbing that, nearly two thousand years later, it should still make every comfortable heart tremble.
The man who appeared to have everything discovered that he had lost what mattered most.
The man who appeared to have nothing was carried by angels into the comfort of Abraham's side.
But before you decide this is simply a story about rich people going to hell and poor people going to heaven, you need to understand something.
That is not what Jesus taught.
And misunderstanding this passage could cause us to miss the very warning He intended us to hear.
Because somewhere between the rich man's expensive clothing and Lazarus's open wounds, Jesus exposed a spiritual danger that can hide inside a respectable life.
A danger that does not always look like cruelty.
Sometimes it looks like indifference.
Sometimes it looks like having enough for yourself while convincing yourself that someone else's suffering is none of your concern.
And sometimes it looks like knowing the Scriptures, speaking religious language, and still refusing to let the mercy of God change the way you live.
The question is not merely whether you have money.
The question is what your relationship with money reveals about your relationship with God.
And the answer may be more uncomfortable than you expect.
In Luke 16:19–31, Jesus begins with a striking description:
“There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day.”
That is Luke 16:19 in the King James Version.

Purple clothing in the ancient world could communicate extraordinary wealth and social distinction. Fine linen suggested luxury. His daily feasting was not an occasional celebration. It was his normal way of life.
Jesus does not tell us how he acquired his wealth.
He does not explicitly accuse him of stealing.
He does not say that every expensive meal was sinful.
Instead, He places something directly outside the rich man's home that changes how we understand everything.
A suffering human being.
Luke 16:20–21 tells us:

“And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores, And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.”
Read that slowly.
Lazarus was not hidden.
He was at the gate.
The rich man did not need to travel across the world to discover suffering.
He did not need to search for an opportunity to show compassion.
Mercy was waiting outside his own door.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us are waiting for God to give us some enormous assignment while overlooking the wounded person already within our reach.
We pray for opportunities to serve.
But sometimes the opportunity has a name.
Sometimes it is the struggling neighbor we avoid.
The elderly parent who needs our patience.
The hungry family we could help.
The person who keeps saying, “I'm okay,” even though their eyes tell a different story.
The church member who stopped attending and nobody bothered to call.
The person who has nothing to offer us in return.
We can become so occupied with protecting our comfort that another person's suffering begins to feel like an interruption.
And perhaps that is one of the most frightening things about the rich man.
Jesus does not describe him standing at the gate, shouting insults at Lazarus.
He does not describe him physically attacking the beggar.
The story simply shows a life of abundance existing beside a life of desperate need.
Yet no act of mercy from the rich man is recorded.
Sometimes the most revealing thing about our hearts is not the evil we openly commit, but the good we repeatedly refuse to do.
James 4:17 warns:
“Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.”
And 1 John 3:17 asks how God's love can dwell in someone who possesses this world's goods, sees a brother in need, and closes his heart against him.
These passages do not teach that every Christian must solve every human problem.
We are finite people with limited resources, responsibilities, and opportunities.
But they do teach that genuine faith cannot remain permanently indifferent to suffering.
Mercy is not a decorative accessory to Christianity.
It is one of the ways a transformed heart becomes visible.
And then Jesus gives us a detail that is easy to overlook.
The rich man is not named.
Lazarus is.
That does not prove the rich man was literally unknown to everyone or that Lazarus had no earthly reputation. Jesus does not explain His reason for naming one and not the other.
But the literary contrast is powerful.
The wealthy man is introduced by his status.
The beggar is introduced by his name.
And that name carries remarkable significance.
Lazarus comes from the Hebrew name אֶלְעָזָר, Elʿazar, commonly understood as “God has helped.”
Think about that.
The man who seemed abandoned by everyone bore a name that testified to God's help.
The man who appeared to possess every advantage had no named identity in Jesus' telling.
In the eyes of society, Lazarus may have looked insignificant.
But in the story Jesus told, he was not forgotten.
There is something deeply comforting here for anyone who has ever felt invisible.
Perhaps you know what it means to struggle while other people celebrate.
Perhaps you have watched others receive opportunities while you quietly wondered whether God had overlooked you.
Perhaps you have prayed for provision and still gone to bed worried about tomorrow.
Lazarus reminds us that earthly circumstances are not a reliable measurement of God's final verdict.
But we must be careful.
His name does not mean God promised him a comfortable earthly life.
His suffering was real.
His hunger was real.
His wounds were real.
And the text never tells us that his poverty was a virtue that earned him salvation.
What Jesus reveals is that the world's judgment of a person's worth can be catastrophically wrong.
A person can be ignored on earth and yet be known to God.
A person can be celebrated on earth and yet stand spiritually bankrupt before Him.
Then the story reaches the moment nobody can postpone forever.
Luke 16:22–23 says:

“And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried; And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom.”
There is a chilling simplicity in those words.
The beggar died.
The rich man also died.
Death did not ask which man owned the larger house.
It did not check their bank accounts.
It did not respect social status.
The rich man could purchase fine linen, but he could not purchase another lifetime.
He could feast every day, but he could not buy his way out of death.
And suddenly the gate that had separated comfort from suffering was replaced by a separation far more serious.
Jesus describes Lazarus being carried to Abraham's side, an image of honor and comfort associated with the faithful patriarch.
The rich man finds himself in torment.
The Greek text of Luke 16:23 uses the word ᾅδης, Hadēs, commonly rendered “Hades,” the realm of the dead. The King James Version translates it “hell.”
That distinction matters.
The Greek word here is not γέεννα, Gehenna, another term Jesus uses in His teaching about final judgment.
Christians differ on how precisely the imagery of Hades, Abraham's side, flame, and the great chasm should be understood in relation to the intermediate state and final judgment.
Some interpret the account as a parable using familiar imagery. Others understand it as a description of actual postmortem realities.
But we must not pretend that every detail answers questions Jesus did not address.
The central warning is unmistakable.
Death does not erase accountability before God, and the opportunity to respond to His revealed truth must not be treated as something we can endlessly postpone.
The rich man had spent his life enjoying what Lazarus lacked.
Now he looked toward Lazarus in comfort while he himself suffered.
And what he said next reveals something deeply troubling.
He cried out:
“Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame.”
Luke 16:24, KJV.
Notice that he recognizes Lazarus.
He knows his name.
That makes the earlier scene at the gate even more haunting.
The story does not explicitly tell us how often the rich man saw Lazarus or what passed through his mind during those encounters.
But now, when the rich man needs relief, he knows exactly whom to ask for.
And he asks Abraham to send Lazarus.
The man who had lain helpless outside his gate is still being spoken of as someone who might be dispatched to meet his needs.
Jesus does not give us enough information to declare every motive in the rich man's heart.
Yet the contrast is unmistakable.
The man who had the resources to show mercy now desperately asks for mercy himself.
And he cannot obtain the relief he requests.
Abraham answers by reminding him of the reversal between their earthly circumstances and their present conditions.
Then he explains that a great chasm has been fixed between them, preventing passage from one side to the other.
That chasm is not presented as a barrier that human determination can overcome.
It exposes the terrible seriousness of the moment.
There are decisions we can postpone.
A purchase.
A vacation.
A career change.
But reconciliation with God is not something Scripture encourages us to leave until after death.
Hebrews 9:27 says:
“And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.”
And 2 Corinthians 6:2 declares:
“Behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”
Not because God delights in terrifying people.
But because His mercy is calling us while we still have breath.
And here is where we must confront a dangerous misunderstanding.
Jesus was not teaching that being wealthy automatically condemns someone or that being poor automatically saves someone.
Abraham himself was wealthy.
Genesis 13:2 describes him as very rich in livestock, silver, and gold.
Yet in Jesus' story, Abraham is the very figure associated with comfort beyond death.
That alone should prevent us from reducing this passage to a simplistic formula.
Wealth is not a substitute for righteousness.
Poverty is not a substitute for faith.
The Gospel does not teach that people can purchase salvation by giving away enough money.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Salvation is God's gift.
Not a reward for financial hardship.
Not a trophy for generosity.
Not a privilege reserved for the wealthy.
And certainly not something earned through religious donations.
But Ephesians does not stop at verse 9.
Verse 10 explains that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us, and that same grace begins transforming the way we live.
A heart changed by Christ cannot regard mercy as permanently optional.
And this is precisely why the context of Luke 16 matters so much.
Before Jesus tells the story of the rich man and Lazarus, He has already spoken about money, faithfulness, and divided loyalty.
In Luke 16:13, He warns:
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon.”
The Greek word μαμωνᾶς, mamōnas, refers to wealth or riches, particularly as something that can become a rival master.
Jesus does not say that possessing money makes a person incapable of loving God.
He warns that money can become something we serve.
Something we trust.
Something we obey.
Something we protect even when obedience to God requires generosity.
Then Luke 16:14 tells us that the Pharisees, who were described as lovers of money, heard these things and ridiculed Him.
Jesus responds by confronting the difference between human approval and God's knowledge of the heart.
That is the immediate setting of the rich man and Lazarus.
The story is not an isolated attack on financial success.
It is part of Jesus' warning against loving wealth, justifying ourselves before people, and ignoring what God has already revealed.
And now the question becomes painfully direct.
What do we love enough to disobey God for?
What do we protect so fiercely that compassion becomes inconvenient?
What would our spending, our generosity, and our treatment of vulnerable people reveal if they were placed beside our public declarations of faith?
It is possible to be financially successful and spiritually generous.
It is also possible to have very little money and still be consumed by greed, envy, or selfishness.
The issue reaches deeper than the amount in our wallets.
It reaches the throne of our hearts.
And whatever occupies that throne will eventually influence how we treat people.
But the most devastating moment in Jesus' story may not be the rich man's request for water.
It comes afterward.
Realizing that his own condition cannot be changed, he asks Abraham to send Lazarus to his father's house.
He has five brothers.
He wants them warned so they will not come to the same place of torment.
For the first time in the narrative, he expresses concern about other people.
But listen carefully to Abraham's response.
“They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.”
Luke 16:29, KJV.
The rich man objects.
He believes that if someone returns from the dead, his brothers will repent.
Then Abraham delivers the final words of the story:
“If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.”
Luke 16:31, KJV.
Those words should stop us.
Because Jesus is revealing that the problem is not always a lack of evidence.
Sometimes it is a refusal to listen to the truth already given.
The Scriptures had spoken about justice.
They had spoken about mercy.
They had spoken about caring for the poor, the stranger, the widow, and the vulnerable.
Deuteronomy 15:7–11 commanded openhanded generosity toward the poor.
Isaiah 58 confronted religious practices that existed alongside oppression and neglect.
Micah 6:8 called God's people to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him.
The rich man's brothers did not need a new revelation before they could begin taking God's commands seriously.
They needed to hear and obey what had already been revealed.
And then there is an extraordinary resonance for those of us reading this story after the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Someone really did rise from the dead.
Jesus.
The crucified Son of God.
The One who was rejected, mocked, pierced, and buried.
The One who rose on the third day.
And yet the New Testament records that even the testimony of His resurrection was met with disbelief by some.
Jesus' closing words in Luke 16 are not a coded prediction that removes the need to understand their immediate context.
But they do confront us with a question that becomes even more urgent in the light of Easter.
If the risen Christ cannot persuade us to surrender our hearts to God, what greater sign are we waiting for?
We live in a world filled with religious content.
Sermons.
Podcasts.
Devotionals.
Bible studies.
Scripture quotations shared across social media.
And all of these can be valuable.
But it is possible to consume biblical information without allowing biblical truth to confront us.
We can listen to a sermon about compassion and still ignore someone who needs help.
We can post a verse about generosity while treating every request for assistance as an inconvenience.
We can speak beautifully about grace while refusing forgiveness to someone who has wounded us.
We can defend sound doctrine while becoming cold toward the people that doctrine calls us to love.
And we can mistake familiarity with Christian language for genuine surrender to Jesus Christ.
That is not a warning merely for wealthy people.
It is a warning for anyone capable of becoming religious without becoming merciful.
Including me.
Including you.
Because the gate in Jesus' story is not only a feature of the rich man's property.
It confronts us with the boundaries we place around our compassion.
The people we allow into our concern.
The suffering we notice.
The suffering we avoid.
The needs we are able to meet but choose not to.
And the uncomfortable truth that sometimes we have enough time to criticize the world but somehow never enough time to love the person standing in front of us.
Yet if we stop here, we have not reached the heart of the Gospel.
Because Jesus did not come merely to tell comfortable people to become more charitable.
He came to rescue sinners.
People whose greed has wounded others.
People whose pride has blinded them.
People whose indifference has hardened over years.
People who have done terrible things.
People who have hidden terrible things.
People who have failed to love when love was required.
People like us.
And that is where this story moves from scandal toward grace.
Not because Jesus minimizes sin.
But because He is the only Savior who can truly deal with it.
The rich man and Lazarus reveal the seriousness of judgment.
The cross reveals the astonishing depth of God's mercy.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ, who was rich in heavenly glory, willingly entered our poverty and suffering for our salvation.
Second Corinthians 8:9 says:
“For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.”
Paul is speaking of the grace of Christ and the spiritual riches made available through His self-giving, not promising that every believer will become financially wealthy.
Jesus did not enter our world to build an earthly empire of luxury.
He came as the suffering Servant.
He welcomed the rejected.
He touched the unclean.
He ate with sinners.
He showed compassion to the poor.
He confronted the self-righteous.
And He laid down His life for those who could never save themselves.
At the cross, the sinless Savior bore our sins.
First Peter 2:24 says that He bore our sins in His own body on the tree.
Romans 5:8 tells us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners.
And through His resurrection, Jesus demonstrated His victory over death.
This is the hope the rich man and Lazarus must drive us toward.
Not merely the fear of dying with the wrong bank balance.
But the urgent need to be reconciled to the living God through Jesus Christ.
Because no amount of money can cleanse a guilty conscience.
No amount of poverty can erase sin.
No amount of charitable giving can purchase eternal life.
Only Jesus saves.
And when He saves, He does not leave us unchanged.
Consider Zacchaeus.
He was a wealthy tax collector, a man whose position was associated with a system that could be exploited for personal gain.
When Jesus entered his life, something changed.
In Luke 19:8, Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his goods to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Jesus then announced that salvation had come to his house.
Zacchaeus did not purchase salvation through generosity.
His response demonstrated the transforming impact of encountering Christ.
The money that once represented his advantage over others became an opportunity for restitution and mercy.
That is what grace can do.
It can turn selfish hands into generous hands.
It can turn a hardened conscience into a tender one.
It can turn someone who once exploited others into someone willing to make things right.
It can teach us that possessions are tools to steward, not gods to worship.
And perhaps you are reading this with a burden in your chest.
Because you remember someone you could have helped.
Someone you ignored.
Someone you treated as unimportant because they had nothing to offer you.
Perhaps you have spent years chasing financial security, only to discover that the more you acquire, the more afraid you become of losing it.
Perhaps you are wealthy and tired of being judged as though success itself were a sin.
Or perhaps you are struggling financially, and you have been made to feel that your hardship proves you lack faith.
Hear this clearly.
Your bank account is not the final measure of your standing before God.
And the solution to spiritual emptiness is not simply becoming richer or poorer.
It is coming to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
If you have sinned through greed, repent.
If you have sinned through indifference, repent.
If you have sinned through envy, repent.
If you have trusted money more than God, repent.
And if you have used religion to excuse a loveless heart, bring even that before Him.

The Greek New Testament uses the verb μετανοέω, metanoeō, for repentance, meaning to repent or change one's mind. In biblical context, genuine repentance involves a changed response to God that bears fruit in the way we live.
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is agreeing with His truth instead of defending your disobedience.
It is trusting His mercy rather than hiding behind your reputation.
And when we come to Christ, we do not come to a Savior who is reluctant to forgive.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive sins and cleanse from unrighteousness when we confess them.
That does not make the consequences of our actions imaginary.
Sometimes repentance requires restitution.
Sometimes it requires an apology.
Sometimes it requires changing our financial priorities.
Sometimes it means opening our hands where we have kept them tightly closed.
But grace means our past failures do not have to be the final chapter of our lives.
That is the beauty of redemption.
The person who once walked past suffering can learn to stop.
The person who once worshiped money can learn to worship God.
The person who once used others can learn to serve them.
The person who once lived for applause can begin living for the glory of Christ.
And now, before you leave this story behind, I want you to imagine one final scene.
Imagine the rich man's gate.
Not as an ancient archaeological detail.
But as something standing in your own life.
On one side are your plans, your responsibilities, your ambitions, your worries, and the things you have worked hard to build.
On the other side is a human being whose need you have the opportunity to recognize.
You may not have the resources to change their entire future.
You may not be able to give them money.
But perhaps you can give them a meal.
A conversation.
A sincere prayer.
A practical referral.
A visit.
A word of encouragement.
A fair opportunity.
A moment of dignity.
Or simply the kindness of being seen.
Not every need is yours to meet.
Not every appeal is wise to support.
Biblical stewardship requires discernment, honesty, and care for those already entrusted to us.
But discernment must never become an excuse for permanent indifference.
And mercy must never become a performance designed to impress an audience.
Jesus calls us to something deeper.
Love that comes from a heart surrendered to God.
Generosity that does not need applause.
Compassion that recognizes the image of God in people whom society has overlooked.
Faith that works through love.
A life that makes the Gospel visible.

And if you are the one lying at the gate, metaphorically speaking—if you are the one struggling, overlooked, exhausted, or waiting for help—please do not hear this story as a command to remain silent in your suffering.
Your need matters.
Your dignity matters.
You are not less valuable because you have less money.
You do not have to pretend everything is fine.
Reach out to trustworthy people and communities who can walk with you.
And remember that Jesus' compassion for the vulnerable is not an afterthought in Scripture.
He sees what the world often refuses to see.
The question for the rest of us is whether we will allow His compassion to shape ours.
Because one day, the achievements that dominate our conversations will no longer matter in the same way.
Our titles will be left behind.
Our possessions will pass into other hands.
The attention we worked so hard to receive will fade.
And we will stand before the God who knows not only what we possessed, but whom we trusted and how we lived.
That truth should humble the wealthy.
It should comfort the overlooked.
It should awaken the indifferent.
And it should send every one of us running to Jesus Christ.
Not because we can earn our place in heaven by becoming sufficiently generous.
But because the Savior who gives eternal life is worthy of our complete surrender.
So here is a question worth carrying into prayer tonight.
Who is the Lazarus at your gate?
Not necessarily someone begging for money.
Someone whose pain you have learned to walk past.
Someone whose struggle you have dismissed.
Someone whose humanity you have stopped noticing.
And what would obedience to Jesus look like if you refused to walk past them again?
Perhaps your first step is not financial.
Perhaps it is repentance.
Perhaps it is a phone call.
Perhaps it is forgiving someone.
Perhaps it is examining the way you use the resources God has entrusted to you.
Perhaps it is asking the Lord to restore a tenderness that disappointment, busyness, or fear has slowly taken away.
Whatever it is, do not confuse being moved by this story with responding to it.
Emotion can fade.
Conviction calls for a response.
If this message has exposed something in your heart, you do not need to pretend otherwise.
You do not have to reveal private details or confess personal sins publicly. God hears the prayers you cannot put into words, too.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who desperately needs this reminder.
Someone who has everything materially but feels spiritually empty.
Someone who has almost nothing and wonders whether God still sees them.
Someone who has become discouraged by hypocrisy.
Someone who needs to discover that Christianity is not about worshiping wealth or romanticizing poverty, but about following the crucified and risen Savior.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, confront difficult truths, and grow closer to Jesus, I want to invite you to consider becoming part of the work that makes this ministry possible.

We want it to be a place where wounded believers find biblical encouragement, where seekers encounter the Gospel, where difficult passages are handled with care, and where people are challenged to move beyond religious appearances into genuine discipleship.
That takes prayer, time, research, writing, resources, and faithful people who believe that sound biblical teaching should continue reaching those who need it.
Think of it as a voluntary ministry offering—one practical way to contribute to the work of sharing Scripture, encouraging believers, and reaching people with the message of Jesus Christ.
But I want to make something unmistakably clear.
Biblical tithes and offerings should never be reduced to a marketing promise, and supporting an online ministry should never be presented as a way to purchase God's favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the kind of support we desire.
Not money extracted through guilt.
But generosity offered freely, thoughtfully, and prayerfully.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Sharing an article with someone who needs it matters.
And the value of your soul has never depended on your ability to contribute financially.
These resources are intended to help you study Scripture, strengthen your understanding of the faith, and continue learning long after you finish reading an article.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown weary, the Christian who feels spiritually distant, and even the person who is still searching for answers about Jesus.
Not because following a page makes anyone a disciple.
But because the truth of God's Word deserves to be heard, studied, tested, believed, and lived.
And perhaps, through one article shared at the right moment, someone will open a Bible they have not touched in years.
Perhaps someone will seek forgiveness.
Perhaps someone will begin making things right.
Perhaps someone who has spent years hiding behind success will finally admit that money cannot heal the emptiness of a soul separated from God.
Perhaps someone who has felt forgotten will discover that the Lord has not lost sight of them.
And perhaps someone will look at the suffering person outside their own gate and finally stop walking.
That is worth praying for.
That is worth sharing the truth for.
That is why this message matters.
Because the rich man and Lazarus is not merely a story about two men who died.
It is a warning to the living.
A warning that wealth cannot save.
A warning that indifference is spiritually dangerous.
A warning that Scripture must be heard and taken seriously.
A warning that death and judgment are real.
But also a reminder that while we still have breath, we are being called to respond to the mercy of God revealed in Jesus Christ.
You are reading this today.
You still have an opportunity to repent.
You still have an opportunity to trust Christ.
You still have an opportunity to make things right where you can.
You still have an opportunity to love someone you once overlooked.
Do not waste that opportunity trying to appear righteous.
Come to the One who alone can make sinners right with God.
Come to Jesus.
The Savior who died.
The Savior who rose.
The Savior who forgives.
The Savior who transforms.
The Savior whose grace is greater than the worst chapter of your past.
And when His mercy reaches your heart, do not keep it imprisoned there.
Let it reach your hands.
Let it reach your home.
Let it reach the person at your gate.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that the rich man eventually lost his wealth.
It is that he reached the end of his earthly life without the kind of response to God's truth that would have changed everything.
One day, the gate you kept walking past will be gone—but the mercy you refused to show may still be the question your conscience remembers.
